title: A microlearning app for peer feedback training and its effect on learning performance and self-confidence during an EFL speaking task
extended_summary:
This study examined whether a mobile microlearning app could improve university students’ peer feedback skills and help them transfer those skills to a related English as a Foreign Language (EFL) speaking task. The authors focused on two questions: whether training students to provide peer feedback through the app improved performance on a constructive communicative language teaching (CLT) speaking activity, and whether students perceived gains in peer feedback, internal feedback, and English-use confidence.

The intervention was Pebasco, a mobile microlearning app designed to train peer feedback on spoken content. Students listened to peer audio clips annotated by the instructor and attempted to predict the timing and nature of teacher comments, with immediate feedback, hints, and repeated practice opportunities. Learning analytics from the app were used to classify students by engagement and success patterns, and these profiles were linked to outcomes on pre/post Flipgrid speaking tasks and end-of-course self-report surveys.

The study took place in a mandatory asynchronous first-year university EFL course in the Faculty of Letters at a Tokyo-based university in Japan. Participants were 89 undergraduate students. The design was a single-group quasi-experimental pre/post study using Flipgrid for performance assessment and Pebasco for training. Students completed an initial speaking video, four units of Pebasco training, and a final speaking video; they also completed an end-of-class Likert-scale survey.

The main findings suggest that active engagement with Pebasco was associated with better outcomes. Students who began with lower initial speaking performance but engaged successfully with the app improved enough to reach posttest performance statistically indistinguishable from initially higher-performing peers. Students who engaged successfully also reported greater perceived improvement in peer feedback skills, internal feedback skills, and in some cases English confidence. The authors conclude that mobile microlearning can support peer feedback training and near transfer to related communicative speaking tasks, though results should be interpreted cautiously given the single-group quasi-experimental design and reliance in part on self-reported measures.

identified_tools.name: Pebasco
identified_tools.description: A mobile microlearning application for peer-feedback training in spoken language learning, providing structured practice around evaluating peer speech and receiving immediate feedback within short learning units.
identified_tools.use_case: Used in a first-year university EFL speaking course in Japan, where students completed four peer-feedback training units in Pebasco between pre- and post-speaking tasks.

findings.finding_summary: Descriptive subgroup results suggest that lower-performing students who ended the Pebasco intervention with stronger user profiles showed greater improvement on the post speaking-task Construction Quality Index than lower-performing peers with weaker end profiles. Exact inferential statistics were not reported in the provided excerpt.
findings.measure: Construction Quality Index on speaking-task videos

findings.finding_summary: Students reported significant self-perceived improvements in peer feedback skills and internal feedback skills, according to the abstract. Exact statistics were not provided in the excerpt.
findings.measure: Self-reported perceived improvement in peer feedback skills and internal feedback skills

findings.finding_summary: The abstract reports improvement in self-confidence during the EFL speaking task / overall English confidence, but the provided excerpt does not include detailed statistics.

quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed quasi-experimental pre/post study with 89 undergraduate students and objective performance measures, but it uses a single-group convenience sample without a control group and is limited to one university context.
impact_tier_rationale: The study reports statistically significant differences with relatively large reported effect sizes (e.g., η² = 0.188 for post performance and 0.143–0.170 for survey outcomes), suggesting meaningful positive impact, though the lack of a control group limits causal certainty.
